# Phase 0: does each expert have a job?

*Feasibility report for [plans/experts-room.md](../../plans/experts-room.md), written 2026-10-30. Numbers, gate checks and expert cards are generated by `tools/moe/report.py`; the prose comes from `tools/moe/narrative.md`.*

## Summary

**The plan's mind, top-2 of 8, fails the gate on (c). The top-1 variant mostly passes it.** In the top-1 variant, each word goes to one expert instead of two. It was trained as an optional extra, on the same data, schedule and seed.

The top-2 mind writes as well as its dense twin, but switching one of its experts off rarely changes stories in a way someone can name and then spot again. The top-1 mind's experts are easier to name, and five of its switch-offs break something specific. With those experts muted, two describer-and-judge models each confirmed all five on fresh story beginnings:
- *"to to to"*;
- broken speech starts;
- *"said said"*;
- *don'* for *don't*;
- *"wanted wanted"*.

| | top-2 (the plan's mind) | top-1 (variant) |
|---|---|---|
| (a) loss vs dense twin | −5.5% ✅ | −3.6% ✅ |
| (b) layers with nameable experts, gpt-6-luna names and scores | 0 of 6 ❌ | 4 of 6 ✅ (also on fresh passages and whole cards) |
| (b) the same, gpt-6.1-sol names and scores | 4 of 6 ✅ | 5 of 6 ✅ |
| (c) rerouted switch-offs, luna describes and judges | 1 ❌ | 2 ❌ |
| (c) rerouted, sol describes and judges | 2 ❌ | 7 ✅ (5 of them confirmed again on fresh beginnings) |
| (c) muted, luna | 2 ❌ | 6 ✅ (5 confirmed again) |
| (c) muted, sol | 3 ❌ | 10 ✅ (8 confirmed again) |

**Top-1 fails only one combination: the plan's own switch (rerouting) judged by gpt-6-luna**, the model this study was set up to use. It got 2 of the 4 needed. Its describer named the apostrophe breakage correctly, but its blind judge matched it 14/20, just short of the cutoff for a second round. Sol matched the same effect 16/20 and then 34/39. All five of the confirmed effects are real; the luna-judged reroute test is just less sensitive to them.

### The top-2 mind (the plan's main run)

- **(a) passes.**
  - The MoE's held-out loss is 5.5% *lower* than the dense twin's (1.417 vs 1.500), at the same active size (13.2M parameters per word) and the same 514M training pieces.
  - In a blind pairwise reading, the judge preferred the MoE's story 60 times out of 96.
  - The router never collapsed: every expert handles between 16% and 36% of words (25% would be even).
- **(b) depends on the scorer.** The test has two model jobs:
  - a **labeler** names each expert and writes its rule;
  - a **scorer** applies the rule to held-out passages, marking which words go to the expert.
  - Results for each pair of models:

    | labeler | scorer | layers passing (3 of 6 needed) |
    |---|---|---|
    | gpt-6-luna | gpt-6-luna | 0 of 6 |
    | gpt-6.1-sol | gpt-6-luna | 2 of 6 |
    | gpt-6-luna | gpt-6.1-sol | 3 of 6 on the first passages, but 1 of 6 on fresh ones |
    | gpt-6.1-sol | gpt-6.1-sol | 4 of 6 on the first passages, on fresh ones, on both pooled, and when scoring the whole card |

  - So the pass is robust only with sol in both jobs, and it comes from layers 3–6. Layer 1 fails everywhere (1–3 of 8). Sol's passing names include:
    - "the naming words expert" (L3·E1, 0.94);
    - "the punctuation expert" (L3·E4, 0.89);
    - "the action expert" (L3·E2, 0.89);
    - "the noun group expert" (L5·E2, 0.88).
  - Sol is the better *scorer* above all. It applies a rule that quotes a dozen pieces plus a context condition more faithfully than luna, and with about a seventh of the reasoning tokens.
- **(c) fails, with either model: 1 rerouted expert qualifies with luna as describer and judge, 2 with sol; 4 are needed.** The test was set before seeing results. Under both models, only one rerouted expert holds up on fresh beginnings, L1·E7 (luna 38/40, sol 40/40).
  - Of 33 specific one-sentence descriptions, the blind matching test certified only one: **L1·E7**. With it off, the word after *to* goes muddled (*"they ran to to to and asked"*). It scored 18/20, then 38/40 on fresh beginnings.
  - Five more came close (15/20). None held up on 40 fresh beginnings. A direct count shows why the test is hard on effects that only sometimes appear:
    - **L1·E0** off breaks apostrophe words in 20 of 48 stories (15 of 40 fresh ones). Switching off any other layer-1 expert does it in 0–2. The effect is real and specific, but it shows up in only about 40% of stories, so the matching test can't certify it (26/40, p = 0.04).
    - **L2·E1**'s doubled *-ed* appeared in 4 of 48 stories and in none of the 40 fresh ones.
  - **Muting** instead of rerouting gives the same picture: 2 qualify by the rule. L1·E7 confirms (34/40). L6·E5 passed round 1 narrowly (15/19), then scored 17/34 on fresh beginnings, which is chance. It was probably the one false pass the test expects.
  - **With gpt-6.1-sol as describer and judge** (same stories, prompts and rules), the answer barely moves:
    - Sol calls fewer descriptions specific (20 rerouted, against luna's 33).
    - Rerouted, 2 qualify:
      - **L1·E7**, as before, confirmed 40/40.
      - **L1·E4** ("more describing, less happening") passed round 1 at 16/20, but scored 25/40 on fresh beginnings.
    - Muted, 3 qualify:
      - L1·E7 again (37/40 on fresh beginnings).
      - **L6·E2** (the word-chunks expert): muted, the mind stutters on word pieces, *"bott bott"*, *"du du"*. That's 11/12, then 21/22 on fresh beginnings, a second effect that holds up firmly.
      - L6·E5, which did not replicate (22/34).
    - Sol couldn't certify L1·E0's apostrophe breakage either (muted: 15/20, then 23/40).

**What the top-2 experts are: word sorters whose lists become grammar roles higher up.**
- **The word decides the route.** A held-out piece goes to its word's usual expert 92% of the time in layer 1, falling to 76% in layer 6. A lookup table of which words go where predicts routing at balanced accuracy 0.83–0.94.
- **In layer 1 the lists are mixed.** No model names them well:
  - L1·E1 gets *was*, *She*, *said*, *day*, *so* and *little*; sol calls it "the was-and-said expert".
  - L1·E7 is "the adventure and chance expert" to luna and "the to expert" to sol.
- **Higher up, the lists line up with grammar roles,** which is why a strong scorer can apply the names there.
- **Names from routing and effects from switching off can disagree.** L1·E7's switch-off shows its real work: *to* and the verb after it.

**What switching off a top-2 expert does.**
- The clearest effects are spelling and grammar breakdowns from layer 1 and layer 2 experts. Each fits in one sentence:
  - **L1·E7** off: the verb after *to* goes missing (*"they ran to to to and asked"*).
  - **L1·E0** off: apostrophe words break (*"Let' go"*, *"It' a surprise"*). On held-out text, predicting the pieces after an apostrophe (*s*, *t*, *re*, *is*) gets 9–11 nats worse.
  - **L2·E1** (the story-verb expert) off: sometimes past tenses get a second ending (*"he wanteded to go out"*). It's vivid but rare.
- **Deeper experts change stories in many small ways, with nothing to name.** Their switch-off costs only 1–3% of the loss. A rerouted expert's words go to a neighbor that can do most of its work. Muting instead of rerouting looks about the same.

The top-2 layers split the two halves of the room. The upper layers have nameable experts whose switch-off barely shows. The bottom layer has visible switch-offs and experts no one can name.

### The top-1 mind (variant)

- **(a) passes.**
  - Held-out loss 1.446, 3.6% lower than the dense twin's, with 7.5% *fewer* active parameters per word (12.2M against 13.2M).
  - In the same blind pairwise reading, the judge preferred its story 57 times out of 96 (the top-2 mind: 60).
  - The top-2 mind is still better (1.417).
  - Early in training the router briefly sent 96% of words to one expert in some layer. It recovered by step 500, and at the end every expert handles 7–20% of words (12.5% would be even).
- **(b) passes with luna alone,** where the top-2 mind got 0 of 6.
  - Layers 3–6 pass on the first passages, on fresh ones, on both pooled, and when scoring the whole card. Sol in both jobs passes 5 of 6, adding layer 2.
  - Layer 1 fails again (1 of 8 with either model).
  - The best names, with both models agreeing:
    - "the sentence-boundary expert" (L4·E1; luna 0.95, sol 1.00 as "the sentence edges expert");
    - "the stop-and-no expert" (L3·E4; 0.93, 0.94);
    - "the character pronouns expert" (L5·E2; 0.90, 0.90);
    - "the story endings expert" (L6·E5; 0.89, 0.91).
  - The names are again grammar roles, not topics.
- **(c): five switch-offs that break something you can name.** Muted, both models certified all five, and each held up on fresh beginnings, between 30/38 and 34/34. Rerouted, sol certified all five and luna two of them (L2·E1 and L3·E1).
  - **L2·E1**, "the place words expert" (sol: "the where words expert"): the mind writes *"to to to"* where the action should be. Its words include *to*, so name and effect agree. It's the strongest effect: 20/20 in round 1 under every model and switch, then 34/34 to 37/37.
  - **L2·E2**, "the storybook phrase expert" (sol: "the quote marks expert"): the first words inside speech marks go missing or come out broken.
  - **L3·E1**, "the character speech expert": speech punctuation breaks and *said* gets repeated.
  - **L3·E2**, "the story punctuation expert": apostrophe words lose their endings (*don'*, *let'*). This is the top-2 mind's L1·E0 effect, now strong enough to certify.
  - **L3·E7**, "the wanting verbs expert": the mind writes *"wanted wanted"* and never gets to what the character wants.
  - A few more passed one model's test but were not confirmed by the other. Examples:
    - L4·E5 (luna: "the pronouns expert"; sol: "the owning words expert"): with it muted, *his mom* becomes *his*, sol only.
    - L5·E4 ("the state and degree expert"): describing words get swapped (*proud* becomes *happy*), luna only.
    - L6·E3 ("the action helper expert"): characters plan different actions after *wanted to*, sol only.
- **Why top-1's switch-offs show more.** With one expert per word, no second expert shares the word's work, and switching an expert off costs more:
  - Layer 2's E1 costs 0.32 nats per word, a fifth of the loss. Two more layer-2 experts cost 0.12–0.13.
  - Every layer-3 expert costs 0.04–0.09, against 0.01–0.04 in the top-2 mind.

  This is the plan's own hedge for small switch-off effects ("Compare top-1"), and it worked.
- **Layer 1 is nearly idle.** Its router is unsure: the chosen expert's weight averages 0.21, where 0.125 would be a coin toss among eight, against 0.44 in layer 3 and 0.71 in layer 6. So each layer-1 expert's output is scaled down to about a fifth. Rerouting six of the eight costs almost nothing (at most 0.004 nats; muting, at most 0.01). Only E0 (0.06) and E6 ("the stops expert", 0.04) matter. The word decides layer-1 routing only 58% of the time, against 80–83% in layers 2–6.

## What this means for the room

**With the top-2 mind** (the plan as written), the switch is the weak part. In layers 3–6, switching an expert off changes stories, but not in a way anyone could name and then spot again. Only a corner is worth building:
- the router's choice for each word;
- the word-sorting finding;
- sol's grammar names for layers 3–6;
- two or three describable switch-offs as challenges.

**With the top-1 mind, the plan's room works, layer 1 aside.** Layers 2–6 have:
- **Cards whose names a model can apply**, in four or five of the six layers, depending on the model. They are grammar names ("the sentence edges expert", "the stop-and-no expert"), as the plan expected.
- **Switches that break something a child can name and then spot again.** Each of these is a ready-made challenge:
  - "Make the mind say *to to to*" (L2·E1).
  - "Make it forget how to write *don't*" (L3·E2).
  - "Make it get stuck on *wanted*" (L3·E7).
  - "Break the quote marks" (L2·E2 or L3·E1).
- **A router a child can test.** In layers 2–6, the word decides the route about 80% of the time, so a child can predict it and then find the context exceptions.

Layer 1 needs a different treatment: an honest "warm-up layer whose router hasn't made up its mind", with routing shown but switches that mostly do nothing. Or hide it.

**Recommendation: build the room on the top-1 mind, with muting as the switch.**
1. **Use `stories-moe-top1.bin`.** It's 3.6% better than the dense twin, uses fewer active parameters, and passes (a) and (b) with the plan's own labeling model.
2. **Make the switch mute the expert** (keep the router's choice, zero the expert's output). For top-1 it is the more natural meaning of "off" for a child. Both models certify five effects that way, and luna, the plan's model, certifies six by the rule. Rerouting can be a second, advanced switch: "send its words to their second choice instead".
3. **Take the card names from gpt-6.1-sol, or from luna for layers 3–6** (both pass there). Write the challenges from the confirmed effects above.
4. **Phase 1's engine must support the gating flag.** Top-1 mixes the chosen expert scaled by its router probability (flags bit 0 = 0), where top-2 renormalizes. See the file format below and the fixture next to the `.bin`.

The top-2 mind isn't needed for the room. It stays useful as a comparison: "two experts per word write a little better but are harder to break".

## Caveats

- **One seed, one size, two routing schemes.** Both use 8 experts with a Switch-style balancing loss. The top-1 result is one training run. It was not repeated, and it came after the top-2 result was known. But the plan named it as the comparison, and every test rule was fixed before the top-1 results came in.
- **The label score is only as good as its scorer.** The plan's test says "a model that sees only the label". With the top-2 mind, the verdict on (b) depends on which model that is. With the top-1 mind, both models pass it. A child applying a name is a weaker reader than either model.
- **The gate (c) test is strict by design.** The describer must name something specific, and a blind judge must then find it on unseen beginnings against a decoy from the same layer. Effects that show up in only some stories cost it power, and the judge model matters. Luna described top-1's apostrophe effect correctly but matched it only 14/20 rerouted.
- **Experts that pass round 1 count even if the confirmation round fails.** That is the rule set in advance; the confirmation round only rescues near-misses. That's why some ✅ rows show an unconvincing confirmation (top-1, sol, rerouted L5·E6: 18/35). The "confirmed again" counts in the summary table leave those out.
- **The first top-1 run had a bug and was discarded.** I mixed the chosen experts by their probabilities renormalized to sum to 1. That's right for top-2, but with one expert the weight is always exactly 1, so the router got no gradient from the language-model loss. Its choices came out nearly flat (top probability 0.14, where uniform is 0.125), and its loss was 3.2% *worse* than the dense twin's. The rerun uses Switch-style gating (the chosen expert scaled by its probability). The top-2 mind is unaffected. Its files are kept as `ckpt-top1-renorm-bug`.
- **The training logs' every-500-steps losses can't be compared between the MoE and the dense twin** (see gate (a)). The comparison uses the full validation set, scored twice (bf16 at the end of training, f32 independently).

Held-out loss is the mean over all 5.17M pieces of TinyStories validation, in 256-piece windows. **MoE vs dense: -5.5%** (gate (a) asks for within about 5%). The every-500-steps losses in the training logs are not comparable between these two runs: they scored the first 40 micro-batches, and the runs used different micro-batch sizes (32 and 16), so they saw different text (fixed since).

Blind pairwise reading of 96 pairs of sampled stories (temperature 0.8, same beginning and seed; judge gpt-6-luna): MoE better 60, dense better 36, tie 0. Mean score 4.3 (MoE) vs 3.7 (dense) out of 10.

The same blind reading for the top-1 variant against the dense twin (96 pairs, same beginnings and seeds): top-1 better 57, dense better 39, tie 0. Mean score 4.4 vs 3.8.

## Gate (b): labels that predict routing

A label passes at balanced accuracy ≥ 0.75; a layer passes when at least 60% of its experts (5 of 8) pass; chance is 0.5. **Label** is the plan's test: the scorer sees only the expert's name and rule. **Card** adds what a child's card would show: the five words it handles most and how busy it is. **Word lookup** is a context-blind baseline: "routed" whenever that piece goes to this expert at least half the time in set A. When the lookup scores well, the expert is mostly a word list. Each score uses 8 held-out passages of 48 pieces per layer (about 96 routed pieces per expert), so it is good to about ±0.03. **Retest** scores the same labels on 8 fresh passages; **pooled** counts both sets together.

| layer | labels passing (median BA) | retest | pooled | cards passing (median BA) | median word-lookup BA | median JS distance | layer passes (label) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2 | 3/8 (0.71) | 3/8 | 3/8 | 3/8 (0.71) | 0.91 | 0.66 | no |
| 3 | 4/8 (0.75) | 4/8 | 4/8 | 4/8 (0.76) | 0.91 | 0.63 | no |
| 4 | 4/8 (0.75) | 3/8 | 3/8 | 4/8 (0.75) | 0.84 | 0.56 | no |

The labeler's own sorting of the 48 jobs: mixed 23, grammar 11, meaning 10, story part 3, word list 1.

## Gate (c): does switching an expert off change stories describably?

Each expert is switched off and the mind rewrites 48 fixed beginnings greedily for 120 pieces. **Reroute** (the room's switch) sets the expert's router score to minus infinity, so its words go to the next-best expert. **Silence** keeps the router's choice but throws the expert's answer away.

The beginnings are split: the describer sees only the even-numbered ones, the matching test uses only the odd-numbered ones. The describer (gpt-6-luna, blind to the expert's label) sees six before/after pairs (earliest-diverging first), the exact first difference in each of its changed stories (the switch-off's direct effect), feature counts over all stories, and the pieces whose prediction suffers most on held-out text. General changes ("the story goes another way", "more repetitive", "more confusing") follow from disturbing any part of the mind, so they do not count: the describer marks a description *specific* only when it names something special to this expert that recurs. Each specific description then faces a **blind matching test**: on up to 20 beginnings the describer never saw, a judge gets the sentence, the normal story, and two switched-off versions (this expert's and a random other expert's from the same layer), and must pick the one the sentence describes. An expert counts for gate (c) when its description is specific, rated at least 3 of 5 for visibility, at least half its stories change, and the matching test passes: at least 12 tests and a hit count chance would reach under 1% of the time (16 of 20). About one false pass is expected across all the tests.

An effect that shows up in only some stories cannot score high on 20 beginnings: where neither version shows it, the judge can only guess. So descriptions that came close (round-1 p < 0.05) get a **confirmation round** on 40 fresh beginnings (the opening words of validation stories no other step reads, such as “Anna loved gum. She liked to chew”), with the same sentence and new decoy draws. It must pass by the same rule on its own data. This round was added after round 1, and its rule (who enters, how it passes) was fixed before its stories were written. Both rounds are shown.

**Reroute: 1 expert qualifies** (33 specific descriptions; 1 on round 1 alone; gate (c) needs at least 4).

| L1·E7 the adventure and chance expert | With this expert off, clear action words like “play,” “eat,” and “see” often turn into muddled or repeated phrases. | 4/5 | 18/20 (p 0.000) | 38/40 (p 0.000) | ✅ |

## All 48 expert cards

Layers are numbered 1–6 from the input; experts 0–7. ✅/❌ is the label score against 0.75. *Busy* is the fraction of all words the router sends to the expert (25% on average with top-2 of 8). *Signature words* go to this expert at least half the time, busiest first. *Lift* is how much more likely a piece is to come here than average. *JS* is the Jensen-Shannon distance between the expert's word distribution and the layer's.

### Layer 1

#### L1·E0 — the word-bits expert ❌

*It catches familiar story words, little pieces inside longer words, and marks like commas and apostrophes.*  
**Rule:** It most often takes the pieces ",", "'", " in", " day", " on", " mom", "my", "ed", " big", " play", " around", and "\"". It also takes bits inside longer words, such as "zz", "aring", "rass", and "rett". For shared pieces, a comma often comes here (86%); " in" is especially likely after "said" before a voice or feeling phrase, while "to" and " a" come here only rarely (9% and 7%).  
**Kind:** mixed

- **Scores for this name:** gpt-6-luna scorer 0.58 · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.66
- **gpt-6.1-sol's name:** the commas-and-chunks expert (gpt-6-luna scorer 0.58 · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.59). *I catch commas, apostrophes, certain everyday words, and little chunks inside longer words.* **Rule:** Its main pieces are ",", "'", " in", " day", " on", " mom", "my", "ed", " big", " play", " around", and "\""; keep leading spaces because they distinguish pieces. It also takes selected word chunks, such as zz in buzzing, rass in embarrassed, rett in regretted, and aring in daring—not words about one particular topic. Commas come here 86% of the time, while " to", " a", and " It" come here 9%, 7%, and 60%; the examples do not reveal when those shared pieces switch experts, so an exact marking rule cannot be recovered.
- **Busy:** 21% of words · JS 0.70 · its top 10 pieces are 36% of its traffic
- **Signature words:** `,` `'` `in` `day` `on` `mom`
- **Most special (lift):** `H` `L` `"` `my` `ave` `round`
- **Score:** label **0.58** (hits 17%, correct rejections 99%; 70 of 384 pieces routed here) · card 0.58 · word lookup 0.94
- **Switch-off cost:** reroute +0.1512 per word (+11.1%), on its own words +0.6590; silence +0.1467 · predictions hurt most: `is` +10.91, `t` +10.10, `re` +9.57, `s` +9.00, `m` +7.84
- **Stories, reroute:** 48/48 change. With this expert off, apostrophe words like “don't” and “it's” often get broken, and some quotation marks come out wrong too. *(specific, matched 15/20, confirmation 26/40, visible 4/5)*
- **Stories, silence:** 48/48 change. With this expert off, little word endings—especially in words like “don’t” and “I’m”—often get dropped or jumbled. *(specific, matched 15/20, confirmation 23/40, visible 3/5)*

*It handles many common words used to tell simple stories.*  
**Rule:** It almost always gets the exact pieces " was", " She", " said", " day", " so", " of", " little", " very", " you", and " be". It also often gets word chunks such as "ig" in "tigers", "ir" in "their", and "est" in "fastest". Shared pieces like " a", " to", and "," come here only sometimes, so their spelling alone cannot tell you to mark them every time.

Other assigned pieces form a word list rather than one meaning or grammar group, including "ir" inside their or squirrel and "est" inside fastest or hardest. Apostrophes and spaces often come here, while a, to, and commas come less often; the evidence does not reveal which contexts select these shared pieces, so an exact marking rule would need more routing information.

**Rule:** It often gets pieces such as " it", ",", " happy", " play", " her", "ed", " up", " him", " went", " day", " girl", and " around". It also tends to get concrete words about animals, their homes or body parts, and nearby actions or feelings, such as " bird", " cage", " mouse", " paw", and " sad". Shared pieces like "it", "her", and "him" fit here when they refer to a character in that kind of scene; a comma by itself is only a weak clue.  
**Kind:** meaning

- **Scores for this name:** gpt-6-luna scorer 0.57 · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.66
- **gpt-6.1-sol's name:** the finishing words expert (gpt-6-luna scorer 0.74 · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.81 ✅). *It handles words and word bits that finish actions, feelings, and little groups of words.* **Rule:** Its strongest regular pieces include " it", " happy", " play", "ed", " up", " him", " went", " around", " smiled", and " back". It also favors object names, feeling words, and word-ending bits, such as the ends of cage, noises, and happily, especially where a phrase finishes before punctuation or a joining word. For shared pieces, favor " it" and " her" when they name who or what an action affects rather than a subject or owner, and "," when it closes a clause before a continuation such as but.

#### L6·E4 — the sentence-boundary expert ❌

*It handles many little words and marks that help story sentences begin and end.*  
**Rule:** Its most common pieces are ".", " the", "⏎", " a", " He", " her", " She", " he", " his", " she", " it", and " The". It also favors sentence-opening words such as "That", "One", "next", and "Every", plus selected pieces of story words such as "c" in crab and "fl" in flame. When shared, " the" and ⏎ almost always come here, " a" usually does, and "." often does; pronouns also come here frequently.  
**Kind:** mixed

- **Scores for this name:** gpt-6-luna scorer 0.75 · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.75 ✅
- **gpt-6.1-sol's name:** the phrase starters expert (gpt-6-luna scorer 0.78 ✅ · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.78 ✅). *I handle little words and word beginnings that introduce people and things, plus sentence breaks.* **Rule:** It usually gets " the", " a", " The", " He", " She", " he", " she", " his", " her", " little", ".", and "⏎". It also favors name beginnings, short opening chunks of words such as crab, kids, lamb, flame, and mum, and words introducing a new time or event. Send the definite articles and line breaks here almost anywhere; periods commonly come here at sentence endings, while pronouns and time-setting words often come here when a clause or new event begins.

- **Signature words:** `.` `the` `'\n'` `a` `He` `her`
- **Most special (lift):** `Some` `ele` `fl` `T` `hin` `Their`

#### L6·E5 — the character subject expert ❌

*It follows story characters, especially when they are the ones doing something.*  
**Rule:** It often gets “ and”, “,”, “ to”, “ he”, “He”, “She”, “.”, “ she”, “ they”, “ day”, “They”, and “ily”. It also tends to get a character’s name or a he/she/they pronoun when that character is the doer or experiencer, often at the start of a sentence; name fragments such as “ily” count too. “and”, “to”, and commas are more likely here near a character’s action or when joining story events; a period is only an occasional, context-dependent choice.  
**Kind:** mixed

- **Scores for this name:** gpt-6-luna scorer 0.69 · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.76 ✅
- **gpt-6.1-sol's name:** the character action expert (gpt-6-luna scorer 0.73 · gpt-6.1-sol scorer 0.75 ✅). *It picks out who acts next and little words that link their actions.* **Rule:** Send almost every " he", " He", " she", " She", " they", " They", and " named" here, and often " and", " to", " day", " time", and "ily". Also look for character names and their ending pieces, especially just before an action, plus words introducing when or where an event happens. Shared connectors and commas come here especially when joining actions or setting up the next event; ordinary sentence-ending full stops usually go elsewhere.

## File format (for Phase 1)

From the docstring of `tools/moe/export.py`:

```text
Export a trained mind to a llama2.c .bin (plus an experts block for a MoE mind).

Dense mind: a plain llama2.c legacy (v0) checkpoint that src/bin-reader.js reads today.

MoE mind ("MoE1" layout; all little-endian, int32 / float32):

  1. llama2.c header, 7 x int32: dim, hidden_dim = 0, n_layers, n_heads, n_kv_heads,
     vocab_size (> 0: classifier tied to the embedding), seq_len.
  2. The usual v0 weights with hidden_dim = 0, so w1/w2/w3 take no space:
     token_embedding [vocab, dim], rms_att [L, dim], wq, wk, wv, wo [L, dim, dim],
     rms_ffn [L, dim], (w1, w2, w3 empty), rms_final [dim],
     freq_cis_real, freq_cis_imag [seq_len, head_size / 2] each (unused, as in run.c).
  3. Experts block, starting right after (2):
     magic b"MoE1", then 7 x int32: version = 1, n_experts, top_k, expert_hidden,
     flags (bit 0 = renormalize the top-k weights to sum to 1), 0, 0.
     router [L, n_experts, dim]            logits = router[l] @ rmsnorm(x)
     w1     [L, n_experts, expert_hidden, dim]
     w2     [L, n_experts, dim, expert_hidden]
     w3     [L, n_experts, expert_hidden, dim]
     expert e's output: w2[l, e] @ (silu(w1[l, e] @ x) * (w3[l, e] @ x)).
  The routing rule: p = softmax(logits); pick the top_k experts by p; weight each by
  p / sum of the chosen p (flags bit 0 set), or by p itself (bit 0 clear, used for top-1);
  the feed-forward output is the weighted sum.

Today's reader rejects a MoE file (its layout sum does not reach the end of the file),
so it can't be mistaken for a dense mind.

Also writes <name>.fixture.json: greedy text and the top logits at every step for a few
prompts, computed in float32 from the exported file, for Phase 1's parity test.

  python tools/moe/export.py C:/Users/toont/tm-data/moe/ckpt/moe/final.pt C:/Users/toont/tm-data/moe/out/stories-moe.bin
```

## Method and settings

- **Training:** 7849 steps × 65,536 pieces (one shuffled pass over TinyStories train, 256-piece windows); AdamW (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 0.1; peak learning rate 0.001 after 300 warmup steps, cosine decay to 0.0001; bf16 autocast; gradient clip 1.0. MoE: load-balancing loss × 0.01, router z-loss × 0.001, dropless top-2 routing. The dense twin uses the same data order, schedule and seed (micro-batches of 32 × 8 for the MoE and 16 × 16 for the dense twin: the same 256 windows per step).
- **Labeling model:** gpt-6-luna for every step. `label.py` prefers gpt-6.1-luna, but on 2026-10-30 `GET /v1/models/gpt-6.1-luna` answered 404 for this key, so it fell back to gpt-6-luna.
- **label:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort high); 48 calls (48 answered from the cache of an earlier run); new calls used 0 prompt + 0 completion tokens (0 reasoning)
- **score:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 384 calls; new calls used 195,048 prompt + 513,502 completion tokens (495,174 reasoning)
- **score-card:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 384 calls; new calls used 207,776 prompt + 495,593 completion tokens (477,862 reasoning)
- **score-retest:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 384 calls (210 answered from the cache of an earlier run); new calls used 89,043 prompt + 250,912 completion tokens (242,135 reasoning)
- **describe:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 48 calls; new calls used 130,261 prompt + 96,949 completion tokens (93,565 reasoning)
- **describe-silence:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 48 calls; new calls used 130,709 prompt + 90,771 completion tokens (87,435 reasoning)
- **verify:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 646 calls; new calls used 308,241 prompt + 263,102 completion tokens (250,739 reasoning)
- **verify-silence:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 564 calls; new calls used 269,566 prompt + 209,209 completion tokens (198,603 reasoning)
- **verify-confirm:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 231 calls; new calls used 109,280 prompt + 112,045 completion tokens (107,372 reasoning)
- **verify-silence-confirm:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 153 calls; new calls used 72,269 prompt + 46,517 completion tokens (43,712 reasoning)
- **judge:** gpt-6-luna (reasoning effort medium); 96 calls; new calls used 32,149 prompt + 13,494 completion tokens (10,902 reasoning)
- **Held-out data:** TinyStories validation, split by story: even-numbered stories (set A) for profiles and the labeler's contexts, odd-numbered (set B) for label scoring and switch-off losses.
- **Label scoring:** per layer, 8 random held-out passages of 48 pieces, the same for all 8 experts of the layer.
- **Reproduce:** see `tools/moe/README.md`.
